h1: 10 Party Planning Tips for a Night Guests Remember
excerpt: Ten practical tips for planning a party, from the guest list and venue to timing the entertainment, so the night runs smoothly and you get to enjoy it too.
intro: Whether it is a 40th in a village hall, a surprise party in a pub function room or a big family celebration in a marquee, the same handful of decisions make the difference between a party that flows and one that stalls. Here are ten tips we have picked up from the parties we work at.

sections.heading: 1. Set the date before anything else
paragraphs: Pick the date first and tell your key people straight away, even before the venue is confirmed. Summer Saturdays and most of December are competitive for venues, caterers and entertainment alike, so an early date gives you choice rather than leftovers. If the guest of honour or close family have fixed commitments, work around those, and avoid clashes with major sporting fixtures that will thin out your guest list.

sections.heading: 2. Write the guest list before you choose the venue
paragraphs: Guest numbers drive everything: the room size, the catering budget, the bar, the seating and how many sessions a photo booth will get through. Write the list early, split it into definite and probable, and plan for the realistic number rather than the hopeful one. A room that is slightly too small feels lively; a room that is far too big feels empty however good the party is.

sections.heading: 3. Visit the venue with a practical eye
paragraphs: Charm matters, but so does the plumbing. On the visit, look for parking and step-free access for older guests and suppliers, the number and location of plug sockets, where the bar sits relative to the dance floor and whether there is a corner for a photo booth. Ask about finishing time, noise limits and whether you can get in early to decorate. Write the answers down; you will have forgotten by the time the quotes arrive.

sections.heading: 4. Decide on a budget and split it early
paragraphs: Agree a total you are comfortable with and divide it between venue, food, drink, entertainment and the extras before you book anything. That stops the first supplier swallowing the lot. Entertainment tends to be squeezed last, which is a mistake, because it is what guests talk about afterwards. Keep a small contingency for the things that only appear in the final week, such as extra decorations, a cake stand or a taxi fund.

sections.heading: 5. Send invitations with the information people actually need
paragraphs: A good invitation answers the questions before they are asked: date, start and finish times, exact address and postcode, parking, dress code, whether children are welcome and how to RSVP. If it is a surprise, say so in large letters. Digital invitations make tracking replies easier; printed ones end up on fridges. Either way, set an RSVP deadline a few weeks before so the caterer gets accurate numbers.

sections.heading: 6. Plan the food around the timings
paragraphs: Hungry guests leave early and drink too fast. Match the food to the length of the party: a sit-down meal for an evening that starts at six, a substantial buffet or street-food style for a later start, and something simple and late, such as bacon rolls, for a party that will run past midnight. Cover dietary requirements on the RSVP so nobody has to ask on the night, and make sure the food comes out before the entertainment peaks.

sections.heading: 7. Build a running order and share it
paragraphs: Even a relaxed party needs a spine. Write a simple timeline: arrivals, food, any speeches or the cake, when the music steps up, when the entertainment starts and last orders. Share it with the venue, the DJ or band, the caterer and whoever is running the photo booth, so everyone knows when their moment is. Leave gaps; the best parts of a party are usually unplanned, but they need space to happen.

sections.heading: 8. Give guests something to do
paragraphs: Dancing suits some guests and terrifies others. Entertainment that works for both groups keeps the whole room involved: a photo booth with props and a guest book, a games table, a cocktail station, a live act for a short set. A photo booth has the extra benefit of sending everyone home with a print and leaving you a guest book of messages. Place it where people pass, not in a far corner, and time it for after the food.

sections.heading: 9. Look after the practical details on the day
paragraphs: Nominate someone who is not the host to handle the day itself: letting suppliers in, dealing with the venue, finding the lighter for the candles, paying the band. Pack a box with tape, scissors, spare extension leads, safety pins, painkillers, phone chargers and a printed copy of the running order and supplier numbers. Arrive early enough that the decorating is finished before the first guest, not as they walk in.

sections.heading: 10. Plan the ending as carefully as the start
paragraphs: How a party ends is how it is remembered. Book taxis or check last train times for guests travelling, arrange somewhere for coats and gifts, and agree with the venue who clears what. Have a plan for the leftovers and the flowers. If you have hired a photo booth, make sure the guest book goes home with you and ask when the digital gallery will arrive. Then, finally, enjoy it; you have earned it.
